title: The container request is too large
steps:
The submit-side YARN client requests an application ID. The ResourceManager (RM) returns its maximum per-container capability.

Spark's Client.verifyClusterResources adds executor heap, configured off-heap memory, overhead, and any explicit PySpark worker memory. It separately checks AM memory plus overhead.

The client throws before submitting the AM launch context if either sum exceeds the maximum. No executor can start for this submission.
trigger: --executor-memory 8g is set on a cluster with an 8 GiB maximum per container. Eight GiB of JVM heap plus any positive overhead already exceeds the limit, even on an otherwise empty cluster.
clue: An application ID is not proof an application was submitted. Look for above the max threshold in the submit process, not an executor log. Waiting for queue capacity cannot fix this error; that is a different condition.
repro: Find the maximum per-container memory of a private test queue. Request exactly that much executor heap, with positive overhead. Check whether the client gets an application ID but never sends the AM launch request.
fix: Lower the sum of heap, overhead, and other counted memory to fit the maximum. The next submission should pass validation; it can still wait for currently available queue capacity.

title: The driver never initializes SparkContext
steps:
The AM starts the user application thread; PythonRunner starts the Python process. Startup logging from the script can therefore be visible already.

The AM waits for the SparkContext initialization signal. It needs the driver's RPC endpoint before registering with the RM and creating the executor allocator.

If spark.yarn.am.waitTime expires, the AM marks the attempt failed for context initialization. A script that exits or throws earlier follows a different path.
trigger: In cluster mode, orders.py blocks on an external dependency before SparkSession.builder.getOrCreate().
clue: Zero executors is expected here: none have been requested. Inspect the AM/driver log for Waiting for spark context initialization and the earlier Python output. Increasing executor count does not make blocked driver code finish.
repro: In a test script, sleep 20 seconds before getOrCreate() and submit with spark.yarn.am.waitTime=5s. Compare the timeout in the AM log with the absence of executor requests.
fix: Move slow initialization after context creation when possible; otherwise allow for measured startup time. Verify AM registration, not merely an early Python print.

title: YARN grants containers but Spark has no executors
steps:
The AM receives a container grant and asks the selected NodeManager (NM) to start the executor with a --driver-url. YARN has fulfilled a placement request, not proved the process can reach the driver.

The executor JVM attempts to fetch the driver's configuration, then register its scheduler endpoint. A bad address can fail at the first RPC, before RegisterExecutor is ever sent.

The driver only schedules work on registered, ready executors. A failed container can be replaced while capacity is still requested, but its replacement receives the same bad address.
trigger: A client-mode driver advertises localhost or another address that the worker nodes cannot reach.
clue: Compare the YARN container list with the Spark UI Executors tab. Inspect the driver URL in executor logs from the worker's point of view. An open driver web UI is not proof the driver RPC endpoint is reachable.
repro: On a multi-host test cluster, use client mode with spark.driver.host=localhost. Compare the driver URL in the executor launch log, the failed bootstrap, and the driver's executor count.
fix: Advertise a worker-reachable submit-host address; configure the local bind address separately if necessary. Verify that registration and LaunchedExecutor succeed.

title: The client-mode driver disappears
steps:
The client-mode AM detects the disconnect. It knows the connection was lost, not whether the external program finished its business logic.

With spark.yarn.am.clientModeTreatDisconnectAsFailed=true, an unexpected disconnect takes the failed path. With the default false and no nonzero exit code reported, the AM can finish with SUCCEEDED.

YARN can clean up cluster containers. It cannot relaunch the external Python driver or recover the stack of the interrupted action.
trigger: The submit-host driver dies, or the AM loses its RPC connection to it without a prior orderly shutdown message.
clue: A successful YARN final status alone does not prove the last write committed. Correlate the AM disconnect message with the submit-host logs and the sink's commit evidence. This behavior is not the cluster-mode restart in case 20.
repro: In a disposable client-mode application, terminate only its own external driver without an orderly shutdown. Compare the AM diagnostics with and without spark.yarn.am.clientModeTreatDisconnectAsFailed=true.
fix: Enable disconnect-as-failure when loss must signal failure. Choose cluster mode if YARN must own driver attempts. Verify that the final report and the actual sink commit agree.

title: A task backlog requests more executors
steps:
The driver's allocation listener observes pending tasks and starts the spark.dynamicAllocation.schedulerBacklogTimeout timer. A brief queue that drains before the deadline need not cause a request.

ExecutorAllocationManager estimates demand from running/pending tasks and executor capacity. With sustained backlog it raises the target in rounds, bounded by demand and configuration; it does not ask for one container per task.

The YARN backend and AM request the new total from the RM. Selected NMs launch JVMs; the new slots become usable only after executors register.
trigger: Dynamic allocation is enabled. A stage exposes hundreds of runnable partitions, but its few existing executors have no free slots.
clue: The driver's target may rise while the live executor count stays flat because the queue has no capacity. Compare the driver's because tasks are backlogged log with YARN grants and actual executor additions.
repro: Use a test queue with spare capacity, dynamic allocation and shuffle tracking, one initial one-core executor, and a maximum of three. Run 12 partitions that each sleep two seconds; set the backlog timeout to one second. Compare requested and live counts over time.
fix: If grants lag requests, inspect queue capacity; if requests never increase, check the target bounds and count runnable partitions. Verify newly registered slots drain pending tasks.

title: An idle executor is or is not removed
steps:
The driver's ExecutorMonitor tracks idleness and deadlines. Cached blocks can use a different idle timeout; with shuffle tracking, an active shuffle can keep its owner from being eligible for removal.

ExecutorAllocationManager considers eligible executors, preserving the configured minimum and the current target. It requests decommissioning when enabled, otherwise removal.

The backend and cluster manager carry out an accepted request. Removing the executor does not stop the driver or end the application.
trigger: A wide stage finishes. One executor has no tasks left but may still hold cached partitions or shuffle data needed by another job.
clue: “No active tasks” and “safe to remove” are different. Check the executor timeline, Storage tab, and dynamic-allocation settings before interpreting an idle JVM as leaked capacity. Loss of an unreplicated cached partition can lead to case 07.
repro: Set spark.dynamicAllocation.minExecutors=0, a 5 s executor idle timeout, and a long cached-executor idle timeout. Materialize a small persisted RDD without a shuffle, wait past 5 s, then unpersist it with blocking=True and wait again.
fix: Release caches when finished, or deliberately retain them. Compare cached blocks and removal reasons before and after; an active tracked shuffle or a minimum executor count can still keep the JVM alive.

title: A persisted partition is missing on the second action
steps:
On the second action, an executor task enters RDD.iterator; because the RDD is persisted, it calls getOrCompute for that partition.

The BlockManager returns an available local or remote block on a hit. With no copy, Spark invokes the computation from lineage, or reads a checkpoint where applicable, and tries to store the result at the selected storage level.

If it cannot retain the new block, the current task can still consume the iterator. Other partitions with valid cached copies keep using them.
trigger: A Python program persists an RDD and calls count() twice. Between the actions, the only usable cached copy of partition 12 is evicted.
clue: persist() is not a guarantee against recomputation or a durable checkpoint. Compare cached partition counts in the Storage tab across the two actions; losing one partition does not imply rebuilding the entire RDD.
repro: Persist and count a small RDD. As an all-block miss control, call unpersist(blocking=True), persist it again, and count. Compare with a third count while the cache is warm. This control does not simulate eviction of just one partition.
fix: Use a storage level appropriate to the reuse pattern, such as memory and disk, and materialize it. Verify cached partition coverage before the next action rather than assuming persist() pinned every block.

title: A filter crosses into Python
route: JVM operator or Python evaluation operator
steps:
The driver's SQL planner can express the first predicate directly in the JVM plan. The second requires a Python evaluation operator whose result the filter can consume.

For the UDF, an executor JVM batches and pickles the selected inputs. A local Python worker executes the function and returns serialized results.

The executor JVM associates the returned values with their input rows and continues the plan. The Python driver does not make a network call per row.
trigger: Compare df.filter(F.col("age") > 18) with a filter that calls an equivalent regular, non-Arrow scalar Python UDF.
clue: Similar-looking Python source can create very different runtime work: the UDF adds a process boundary, conversion, and serialization. Compare df.explain("formatted") for BatchEvalPython; Arrow and pandas UDFs use other paths.
repro: Run the same nullable fixture through age > 18 and a Boolean scalar Python UDF with equivalent null handling and useArrow=False. Inspect the formatted plans and collect the small outputs.
fix: Use a built-in expression where semantics match. Verify identical results, including null cases, and the disappearance of BatchEvalPython; do not infer speedup solely from syntax.

title: A small dimension table is broadcast
steps:
The SQL planner selects a build side and requires it in hashed broadcast form. The physical plan identifies which child is built and which is streamed.

The build-side exchange materializes the relation for broadcast. Executor tasks on the streamed side obtain the broadcast value and probe it with their local input rows.

This join need not repartition the large input by join key. Upstream or downstream operators can still shuffle for their own reasons.
trigger: An orders table joins a small regions table on region_id. Join type and size estimates, or an applicable hint, allow a broadcast hash join.
clue: Broadcasting can save a large shuffle but requires space to build and distribute the relation. A “small” row count alone is not proof it fits. Look for BroadcastHashJoin, BuildLeft/BuildRight, and BroadcastExchange in the physical plan.
repro: Join spark.range(1000) to F.broadcast(spark.range(10)) on id; materialize the result and inspect the final plan. Ten matching keys are expected. Compare with an unhinted run.
fix: Broadcast only a measured build side that fits. If it is too large, remove the hint and inspect the alternative plan. Verify the build side and result count, not merely a lower stage count.

title: AQE splits a skewed join partition
steps:
After shuffle stages materialize, the adaptive optimizer reads actual map output statistics. A candidate must exceed both the configured absolute threshold and the median partition size times the skew factor.

For an eligible join side with splittable data, OptimizeSkewedJoin builds smaller shuffle-read specifications. Each gets the corresponding data from the other side; that matching data may be read repeatedly.

If the rewrite satisfies the plan's distribution requirements, executors run the new partition pairings instead of one oversized task.
trigger: An eligible sort-merge join has one very large reducer partition for a popular key. Adaptive Query Execution (AQE) and skew-join handling are enabled.
clue: Tail latency can fall at the cost of extra reads and tasks. Not every big partition is splittable or eligible. Inspect the final adaptive plan and skewed shuffle reads, not just the pre-execution plan. Unlike case 13, this changes the division of work instead of duplicating the same task.
repro: In a test session disable automatic broadcast, enable AQE/skew join, and use eight shuffle partitions. Spread a heavily repeated key over many map partitions, include several smaller keys, and join to a unique-key dimension. Lower the skew-size threshold for this small fixture and inspect the final plan after the action.
fix: First verify the input skew and eligibility. If Spark splits it, compare maximum task read size/duration against the median and confirm row counts are unchanged. A hot key in one unsplittable map block may need upstream repartitioning or a different key strategy.

title: A reducer cannot fetch a shuffle block
steps:
The reduce executor reports FetchFailed. The DAGScheduler checks that the report belongs to the current stage attempt; an old report need not trigger another recovery.

The driver marks the consuming attempt failed and invalidates affected map-output metadata. It queues the producer and consumer stages for resubmission, subject to the stage-failure limit.

Executors regenerate missing map output. The retried consumer can now fetch from its new location. Already available map outputs need not all be regenerated.
trigger: A reducer needs a remote map output. Its serving node or files are gone, and fetch retries cannot deliver the bytes. Assume a normal, durable shuffle.
clue: Retrying only the reducer against the old address would not help. Look for FetchFailed followed by stage resubmission and new map task attempts. Executor exit alone does not imply data loss if an external shuffle service still serves the files.
repro: Use DAGSchedulerSuite's run trivial shuffle with fetch failure fixture: finish the map stage, inject a fetch failure for the current consumer attempt, then complete the resubmitted work. Compare the producer location and stage attempt IDs before and after.
fix: Correlate the missing producer block with executor, disk, and shuffle-service logs. Restore a reliable serving path; verify both regenerated map output and a successful downstream retry. More fetch retries cannot recreate a deleted file.

title: The same partition fails on every attempt
steps:
The Python worker/executor reports a task failure. The driver's TaskSetManager classifies the reason and increments the counter for this partition index if the reason counts toward task failures.

Below the limit the task goes back on the pending list. Another executor can run it, but sees the same input and code.

Once the effective spark.task.maxFailures threshold is reached, the driver aborts the task set and the dependent job fails. With a limit of four, that is four counted failed attempts, not four retries after the first.
trigger: A Python mapping function raises an ordinary data-dependent exception whenever it encounters one malformed record in partition 12.
clue: More executors will not repair a deterministic bad record. Compare the partition index, attempt IDs, and Python exception across hosts. The action fails; whether the application ends depends on what the driver does with that exception.
repro: With spark.task.maxFailures=2, run sc.parallelize(['1','bad','3'], 3).map(int).collect() on a test YARN application. Match the bad partition and ValueError across attempts.
fix: Validate or quarantine bad records before conversion; record rejected rows explicitly. Re-run the fixture and account for two accepted rows and one rejection, without repeated task failures.

title: A slow task gets a speculative copy
steps:
The scheduler periodically checks running attempts. TaskSetManager applies timing and eligibility checks and marks a qualifying task as speculatable.

Given a suitable resource offer, the driver launches a second attempt for the same partition while the original is still running.

The first accepted success wins. The driver requests cancellation of any still-running sibling and does not count a late duplicate as a second result.
trigger: With spark.speculation enabled, one task continues running far longer than its eligible peers. No task failure has been reported.
clue: The job consumes one logical result, but both attempts may already have performed external side effects. A direct database insert inside foreachPartition is not made exactly-once by speculation. Look for distinct attempt IDs for the same task index and a sibling killed after success.
repro: Replay TaskSetManagerSuite's SPARK-26755 Ensure that a speculative task is submitted only once for execution. Observe two attempt IDs for one partition and a single logical result. For logs from a real run, match attempts by stage and partition.
fix: If duplicate side effects are the problem, use an idempotent key or a commit protocol; disabling speculation alone does not eliminate normal retries. Verify one committed logical record per key.

title: The driver stops hearing executor heartbeats
steps:
The driver's HeartbeatReceiver compares the last-seen time to its timeout on a periodic expiry check. One late heartbeat is not an immediate declaration that the node died.

On expiry, the driver asynchronously asks to kill and replace the executor. It also notifies the coarse-grained scheduler backend to remove the executor rather than waiting indefinitely for an RPC disconnect.

The task scheduler can now fail or reschedule attempts assigned there; a replacement still needs YARN capacity and must register with the driver.
trigger: An executor stops sending timely Spark heartbeats, for example during a prolonged process pause or a network interruption. Its NM may still be heartbeating to YARN.
clue: Executor heartbeat timed out proves the driver did not hear from the executor in time, not that the entire host failed. Compare Spark timestamps with NM/container health and the executor's GC logs.
repro: Use HeartbeatReceiverSuite's expire dead hosts fixture: register a test executor, advance its test clock without an update, and run expiry. Repeat with an intervening heartbeat as the control.
fix: Check GC pauses, CPU starvation and the executor-to-driver network path before increasing timeouts. Verify last-seen timestamps recover and replacements stop; a healthy NM heartbeat is not the control for Spark RPC.

title: YARN preempts a healthy executor
steps:
YARN ends the container and reports PREEMPTED to the AM through its allocation cycle. The Spark user's task need not have done anything wrong.

YarnAllocator records the container loss as exitCausedByApp=false and provides the loss reason to the driver.

A running ordinary task can be retried. When that reason reaches it, TaskSetManager does not charge the executor loss against that task's normal failure budget. The AM can request replacement capacity if needed.
trigger: The YARN scheduler reclaims an executor container for resource sharing while it is running tasks.
clue: Work already done by interrupted tasks can be lost even though the failure is not charged to the code. Check for was preempted in the AM log before chasing a Python exception or increasing spark.task.maxFailures.
repro: Use the completed-container fixture in YarnAllocatorSuite (SPARK-26269). Feed a completion with PREEMPTED and inspect the allocator's reason; compare it with the memory-limit completion in case 16. No real queue preemption is needed.
fix: If losses repeat, inspect queue policy and usable capacity, not just task code. Check that replacement executors register and lost work finishes without repeatedly charging application failures.

title: YARN kills an executor for exceeding physical memory
steps:
The NM/YARN terminates the container and supplies a physical-memory exit status and diagnostics to the AM.

YarnAllocator recognizes KILLED_EXCEEDED_PMEM, extracts available usage details, and marks the exit exitCausedByApp=true, unlike preemption.

The driver removes the executor. Ordinary tasks lost for this reason can count toward their failure limits; running the same oversized partition on an identical replacement can repeat the kill.
trigger: The executor's container exceeds its enforced physical-memory limit. Python workers, JVM heap, and native allocations can contribute; a JVM OutOfMemoryError is not required.
clue: Inspect the container's physical usage/limit and partition sizes, not just the Spark UI's storage-memory chart. Contrast case 01 (the request was never accepted) and case 15 (capacity was reclaimed, not exceeded).
repro: In the same allocator fixture, submit a synthetic KILLED_EXCEEDED_PMEM completion. Correlate its classification with a historical container report showing physical memory usage. Do not exhaust a shared node to reproduce this.
fix: Measure container RSS, including Python and native work, and locate oversized partitions. Reduce the working set or adjust overhead within YARN limits. Verify comparable data completes without another physical-memory kill.

title: Collect exceeds the driver result limit
steps:
Executors serialize partition results. A small result can travel in the task status message. A larger permitted result may be stored as a block, with a reference sent to the driver instead.

The driver's TaskResultGetter / TaskSetManager account for serialized result sizes. For this result stage, the cumulative positive limit applies regardless of direct or indirect transport.

Once the total exceeds the limit, the driver aborts the task set. Python does not receive a partial list as a successful collect().
trigger: A PySpark RDD collect() requests every record. Suppose 100 partitions each return about 6 MiB serialized, with spark.driver.maxResultSize set to 512 MiB. Every partition fits individually; their total does not.
clue: The driver error refers to the total size of serialized results. Spreading identical output over more partitions or fetching via block managers does not reduce that total. A limit of zero disables the guard, not the driver's physical memory limit.
repro: Use a fresh test context with spark.driver.maxResultSize=1m. Collect several partitions of small, distinct byte arrays well under 1 MiB each but over 1 MiB together. Read the error's serialized-byte total; compression affects the required sample size.
fix: Aggregate or write distributed output and return only a bounded summary. Confirm the expected aggregate without materializing all rows in Python. Raising the limit does not create driver memory.

title: All write tasks succeed but the job commit fails
steps:
On each executor, the writer creates task output and commits that task through the commit protocol. Successful commit messages return to the driver.

The driver's FileFormatWriter invokes job-level commit using those messages. The Hadoop committer/filesystem now has to finalize the output.

If this throws, Spark attempts job abort/cleanup and propagates the failure. A task failure earlier in the sequence would instead enter task-abort handling.
trigger: A V1 Hadoop-backed file write, such as a Parquet write using that path, finishes its output tasks but encounters a filesystem error during commitJob.
clue: Green tasks do not prove the dataset was published. Check driver commit/abort logs and the destination before retrying. Cleanup is committer- and filesystem-dependent; do not assume universal atomic rollback or extend this V1 behavior to every transactional table format.
repro: Use ParquetIOSuite's JobCommitFailureParquetOutputCommitter with a scratch output path. Its injected failure is in commitJob, not commitTask. Compare successful task commits with the driver exception.
fix: Correct the filesystem or committer cause and inspect partial output before retrying. Verify a fresh read of the intended dataset after successful job commit, not just green tasks.

title: One job group is cancelled in a shared application
steps:
The DAGScheduler uses the captured job-group property to find matching jobs. The ordinary cancellation targets the group currently submitted; it does not permanently forbid reuse of the same group ID.

For a matching job, the driver finds running stages that belong only to that job and asks the task scheduler to kill their attempts. A stage still needed by another active job is not cancelled on that basis.

The cancelled job's caller receives failure/cancellation. The SparkContext, unrelated jobs, and YARN application can continue.
trigger: Two clients share a Spark application, or two submitting threads run jobs under different group IDs. The driver calls sc.cancelJobGroup("report-A").
clue: A job marked cancelled beside a still-running shared stage is consistent. Killing the entire YARN application would have a much wider effect. Check group IDs and stage ownership in addition to the app's YARN state.
repro: Run two bounded slow jobs from separate submitting threads with distinct group IDs. Set the group in each submitting thread and cancel only one while both are active. Compare job states in the UI.
fix: Bind group IDs to requests and clear thread-local properties when reusing threads. Verify the chosen action was cancelled, the unrelated action completed, and the same context accepts another job.

title: The cluster-mode AM crashes and YARN retries it
steps:
The RM detects the lost attempt. spark.yarn.maxAppAttempts cannot grant more attempts than yarn.resourcemanager.am.max-attempts. Spark's AM shutdown path distinguishes terminal cleanup from leaving room for a retry.

For an eligible retry, YARN starts a fresh AM container for the same application ID with a new attempt ID. It does not restore the old JVM.

The new AM and Python driver run the user application from its entry point, create a new context, and obtain executors. Durable files may survive; Python variables, cached driver state, and the interrupted call stack do not.
trigger: The cluster-mode AM/driver container dies before it can report success. YARN policy and remaining attempt budget allow another attempt.
clue: If the first attempt appended records before it died, rerunning the script can append them again unless the application or sink prevents duplicates. Correlate logs by attempt ID, not just application ID. This is a whole-driver restart, not the task retry in case 12 or the stage repair in case 11.
repro: In a disposable managed YARN test with two AM attempts allowed, log an entry-point marker and run a bounded, long-enough action. Have the mini-cluster harness fail only the first AM container, not the application. Use yarn applicationattempt -list to compare attempt IDs and entry markers.
fix: Fix the AM loss reason and make publication idempotent across attempts. Verify one logical output under the same application ID even though the script entered twice. Changing task retry limits cannot restore the old driver.

title: Every submission uploads the Spark JARs
steps:
The submit-side YARN client finds the local Spark JAR directory, creates a temporary ZIP, and adds its readable .jar files.

The client stages that ZIP and declares it as an ARCHIVE resource named __spark_libs__. The NodeManager localizes it for the container; the ResourceManager does not stream JARs.

A reusable archive on cluster-accessible storage changes this path: Spark declares the supplied archive instead of rebuilding it from the local installation for every submission.
trigger: Even a tiny orders.py takes a long time to submit. Neither spark.yarn.archive nor spark.yarn.jars is configured.
clue: Look for falling back to uploading libraries under SPARK_HOME in the submission log. This delay precedes executor allocation; adding executors won't shorten it.
repro: Submit a minimal script without either Spark-JAR setting. Inspect the fallback warning and staged archive; then submit the same script using a compatible prebuilt spark.yarn.archive on HDFS.
fix: Store versioned, cluster-readable Spark archives with JARs at the archive root. Verify the fallback warning disappears and the AM loads the intended classes. Measure submission time separately from executor startup.

title: Spark-submit exits before the report is ready
steps:
The client submits the application and obtains an application ID.

On the fire-and-forget path without a connected launcher backend, the client reads one application report. It throws if YARN already reports FAILED or KILLED; otherwise it can exit without waiting for a terminal result.

The AM, driver, and executors continue independently. The output commit and even a later application failure can occur after the shell has started its next command.
trigger: A shell pipeline starts a downstream reader as soon as a cluster-mode spark-submit command exits zero. It used spark.yarn.submit.waitAppCompletion=false.
clue: A submit log ending with an ACCEPTED or RUNNING report is not a completion receipt. Use the application ID to check final status, or retain completion monitoring when the next step depends on published output.
repro: Submit a script with a brief delay before a scratch output write, using spark.yarn.submit.waitAppCompletion=false. Record shell exit, YARN state, and first readable output. Repeat with the setting true.
fix: Make the consumer wait for terminal success and the sink's publication condition, or retain client monitoring. Verify the downstream reader cannot start against an incomplete dataset.

title: A module imports on the driver but not on workers
steps:
The driver and executor-side Python workers have separate import paths. An import succeeding on the AM node establishes nothing about the worker nodes.

For future tasks, sc.addPyFile("hdfs:///deps/pricing_rules_v2.zip") registers the file and records its archive name among the Python includes. The ZIP must contain an importable pricing_rules package or module.

Worker setup adds its localized Spark-files root and included archives to sys.path before executing the Python command. This distributes Python code, not a Python interpreter.
trigger: The driver imports a local pure-Python helper, but an RDD function doing import pricing_rules raises ModuleNotFoundError on an executor.
clue: Compare the module path on the driver with the import traceback in executor logs. Register the dependency before the affected action; adding the same path again is not an in-place package upgrade.
repro: Use a unique test module name installed only beside the driver script. Import it inside an RDD function. After observing the worker import error, put the module at the root of a versioned ZIP and pass it with --py-files on the next submission.
fix: Distribute the pure-Python dependency rather than editing one host. Return the module's version from each partition and verify the worker results, not just the driver's import.

title: A Python worker rejects the driver version
steps:
The executor JVM starts a Python worker for the Python operation and supplies the expected driver Python version during initialization.

The worker compares it with its own major.minor before deserializing the user function. The mismatch raises PYTHON_VERSION_MISMATCH; the function body never runs.

A retry on a node with the same mismatch fails for the same reason. A JVM-only SQL operation can succeed because it does not perform this worker handshake.
trigger: A built-in DataFrame aggregation succeeds, but a Python RDD task fails when the AM's Python driver uses Python 3.11 and the worker starts Python 3.12.
clue: The error names the worker and driver versions. Check the executables selected inside the containers; Python patch-level differences alone are not this check.
repro: In a private test environment with two supported Python minors already installed, select one for the driver and the other for executors. Run a JVM-only expression, then sc.parallelize([1]).map(lambda x: x+1).collect().
fix: Point the containers to a consistent interpreter or packaged environment. Return sys.version_info[:2] from a worker and compare it to the driver, then verify the Python action returns [2].

title: A closure captures the SparkContext
route: SparkContext pickling guard; no worker execution
steps:
When preparing the Python command, the driver serializes the function and captured objects with CloudPickleSerializer.

SparkContext.__getnewargs__ deliberately rejects pickling the context. Preparation fails on the driver, before an executor can run this function.

Reading app_id = sc.applicationId on the driver and capturing only app_id removes that dependency. The worker receives data, not access to the driver's scheduler.
trigger: A Python RDD transformation contains lambda row: (sc.applicationId, row). The programmer only wanted a string, but the function references the driver context itself.
clue: Look for CONTEXT_ONLY_VALID_ON_DRIVER in the serialization traceback, not four failed task attempts. Increasing the task retry limit does not fix this error.
repro: Evaluate sc.parallelize([1]).map(lambda x: (sc.applicationId, x)).collect(). Then assign app_id = sc.applicationId outside the lambda and repeat using app_id.
fix: Capture the small value rather than sc, spark, or an object holding either. Verify the second closure returns the expected pair and the first failed before the task could execute.

title: Local iteration still needs room for a partition
steps:
As the Python consumer requests more data, the driver JVM submits a job for a partition. The partition computation materializes its result as an array.

The JVM waits for that partition and serves its elements to Python over a local socket. With prefetchPartitions=True, it can submit the next partition job before finishing this one.

Consumption can stop early. If the consumer instead calls list() on the iterator, Python again retains the entire result.
trigger: A report switches from rdd.collect() to rdd.toLocalIterator() to avoid holding the whole result, but one exceptionally large partition still overwhelms the driver.
clue: Expect successive partition jobs, not one RPC per row. Budget for the largest partition (potentially two with prefetch); limiting driver retention is not a guarantee that an individual partition result fits.
repro: Iterate over sc.parallelize(range(8), 4).toLocalIterator(prefetchPartitions=False) one element at a time and observe jobs. Repeat with prefetch on and compare the timing of the next partition job.
fix: Consume incrementally; do not rebuild a list. If a single partition is oversized, change partitioning or keep processing distributed. Verify bounded partition sizes and equivalent output counts.

title: Taking three records starts several jobs
steps:
PySpark's driver starts by asking runJob to scan one partition. Each selected partition returns at most the number of records still needed.

If the batch found nothing, the driver increases the number of partitions to try; if it found too few, it estimates the next batch from the hit rate.

It stops when it has enough records or has scanned every partition, and returns at most three records. A shuffle dependency upstream can still require broader map-side work.
trigger: rdd.filter(is_late).take(3) runs on an RDD whose early partitions contain no late records. The Jobs tab shows multiple successful jobs.
clue: Several jobs at the same take call site, with no failed attempts, can be intentional. take(3) limits the result size, not how much input must be searched.
repro: Run sc.parallelize(range(100), 100).filter(lambda x: x >= 90).take(3). Compare with x < 10 on the same input. Both return three rows, but the late-match run scans farther.
fix: For an inspection sample, accept the extra search. For recurring large scans, prune or index the source where possible. Verify reduced input work rather than raising the requested sample size.

title: A window query sends every row to one partition
steps:
The driver's WindowExecBase requires AllTuples for an empty partition specification. With multiple input partitions Spark inserts an exchange to bring all rows together and sorts the input as required.

A single executor task evaluates the global window. Adding workers or calling repartition(8) before the window cannot remove the distribution requirement.

A keyed window requires clustered distribution by key instead. It is a valid alternative only if the intended answer is a ranking per key rather than a global ranking.
trigger: A report computes a row number ordered by time, without specifying a window partition. There are eight input partitions but one task at the window.
clue: Exchange SinglePartition and the No Partition Defined warning point to operator semantics, not missing YARN capacity.
repro: Use df = spark.range(64, numPartitions=8) and row_number().over(Window.orderBy('id')) (from pyspark.sql.functions and pyspark.sql.window). Select the rank and collect the small result so the optimizer cannot prune the window. Inspect the exchange and task count.
fix: If ranks should restart per customer, use Window.partitionBy('customer').orderBy('id') on a keyed fixture. Verify rank 1 per customer and the disappearance of the global-window requirement. Do not change the key if the required rank is genuinely global.

title: Grouping values moves more data than summing them
steps:
PySpark's map-side Python workers can combine values locally for groupByKey, but the combiner is a list of values. Local packing does not eliminate the amounts.

With reduceByKey(add), the map-side combiner keeps a partial sum per key instead. When repartitioning is necessary, workers shuffle the partials and merge them by key.

Repeated keys within a partition can therefore reduce shuffle volume substantially. Changing to reduceByKey is appropriate for an associative, commutative reduction, not for callers that need all original values.
trigger: A pair RDD has many (region, amount) records per input partition. The code uses groupByKey().mapValues(sum); the only desired result is one sum per region.
clue: Compare shuffle bytes, not just final row counts or task counts. A single hot key still belongs to one final reduce partition.
repro: Build pairs = sc.parallelize(range(20000), 8).map(lambda i: (i % 4, 1)). Compare pairs.groupByKey().mapValues(sum) and pairs.reduceByKey(lambda a,b: a+b). Materialize both and read shuffle metrics.
fix: For this sum, use reduceByKey. Verify all four totals are 5,000. Compare measured shuffle bytes on the same inputs rather than assuming a fixed reduction ratio.

title: Coalescing to one leaves most cores idle
steps:
Without a shuffle the driver constructs a CoalescedRDD with a narrow dependency. The one output partition can walk many parent partitions.

One executor task can consequently evaluate the narrow upstream chain and write the output. There are no other ready partitions of that stage for idle cores to take.

Shuffling (for example, repartition(1)) lets upstream tasks run in parallel before a single final partition. It buys parallelism at the cost of a shuffle, not a parallel final writer.
trigger: A narrow, uncached RDD pipeline ends with coalesce(1) before a save. YARN shows plenty of executors, but one task does most of the work.
clue: Compare the stage DAG and number of tasks before requesting more containers. A one-task stage is a work-partitioning limit, not necessarily a YARN shortage.
repro: Compare sc.parallelize(range(1000), 8).map(str).coalesce(1) with the same pipeline using repartition(1); save to two fresh scratch paths. Inspect upstream versus final-stage task counts.
fix: Avoid forcing one output partition unless the consumer requires it. If it does, shuffle later, after expensive parallel work; verify output equivalence and where the one-task stage now begins.

title: A reliable checkpoint is empty until an action
steps:
The driver has marked the RDD for checkpointing; it has not eagerly written its partitions.

After an action on that RDD, the checkpoint path runs a job to write partition data to the reliable filesystem. An uncached parent can be computed again during this write.

After successful materialization Spark installs a checkpoint RDD as the new parent and clears the original dependencies. This differs from eviction of a cache block in case 07.
trigger: The driver calls sc.setCheckpointDir(...) on shared storage and rdd.checkpoint() before its first action. rdd.getCheckpointFile() still returns None.
clue: Compare getCheckpointFile() before and after count(), or look for Done checkpointing RDD in the driver log. These files checkpoint the RDD, not the Python driver's variables or the YARN application attempt.
repro: Set a fresh HDFS checkpoint directory; persist a small RDD, call checkpoint() before its first action and inspect getCheckpointFile(). Call count() and inspect it again.
fix: For durable lineage truncation, use accessible reliable storage and wait for materialization. Verify the returned checkpoint path and the shortened dependency chain; use persistence alone if the goal is only faster reuse.

title: A task spills to disk and still succeeds
steps:
The executor's sorter checks its estimated collection size. At its memory threshold it requests more execution memory; insufficient growth can trigger a spill. A forced-spill threshold is another route.

The sorter writes an intermediate run to local disk, releases execution memory, and continues. It can read and merge spilled data when producing its output.

The task records memory and disk spill metrics. The estimated in-memory bytes released and serialized bytes actually written are different measures.
trigger: A JVM-side operation using ExternalSorter builds a collection that needs more execution memory than the task can obtain. The task is not killed.
clue: A successful stage can show both spill metrics and spend time in disk I/O. This is neither a YARN memory-limit kill (case 16) nor evidence that an RDD cache block was evicted.
repro: Use ExternalSorterSuite's spilling with hash collisions: it lowers the element spill threshold for a bounded fixture. Compare sorted/aggregated output and the spill path with a control that fits in memory.
fix: For repeated costly spill, reduce records per partition or combine earlier before adding memory. Compare spill bytes and duration and identical output. A modest spill on a successful task needs no corrective action.

title: A broadcast works after unpersist but not after destroy
steps:
unpersist() asks Spark to remove the broadcast blocks from executors, leaving the driver-side broadcast valid. A later action can fetch those pieces again.

destroy() invalidates the driver's broadcast handle and also requests removal of driver-side state. Spark checks validity when serializing that handle again.

A new closure using the destroyed broadcast cannot rely on it. To use the lookup again after destruction, create a new broadcast. Blocking cleanup changes waiting, not validity.
trigger: Two actions use rates = sc.broadcast(lookup). The driver calls rates.unpersist() or rates.destroy() between actions, expecting identical behavior.
clue: Failure preparing a later task that captures a destroyed broadcast is different from a live broadcast being fetched again after unpersist(). This is a user-created broadcast variable, not a SQL broadcast-join planning choice.
repro: Broadcast a small dictionary, look it up in an RDD action, call unpersist(blocking=True), and repeat. Then destroy(blocking=True) and submit a new closure using the same handle.
fix: Use unpersist for evictable, reusable data and destroy only after its last consumer. Create a fresh broadcast for subsequent jobs and verify equal lookup results.

title: An adaptive shuffle has fewer reader tasks than expected
section: Adaptive plans, schemas, and file scans
steps:
Once shuffle map statistics are available, the driver's adaptive rule considers compatible shuffle stages together, using bytes per partition, target size, and parallelism constraints.

Where useful, it builds new read specifications that group reducer partitions and rewrites the shuffle read. It need not rerun the map tasks to write fewer buckets.

Downstream tasks read the groups. Unlike skew splitting in case 10, this combines small partitions to reduce scheduling overhead; it does not request fewer executor containers.
trigger: An eligible SQL aggregation is planned with 200 shuffle partitions, but after filtering, most shuffle outputs are tiny. AQE and shuffle partition coalescing are enabled.
clue: Inspect the final adaptive SQL plan for a coalesced AQEShuffleRead and compare map and reader task counts. An advisory size isn't a promise of a precise count.
repro: Group a small spark.range with multiple input partitions by id % 5 using 200 initial SQL shuffle partitions. Execute with AQE enabled; compare the final adaptive plan with coalescing enabled and disabled.
fix: If the smaller reader stage is faster and the five totals match, keep it. If tasks become too large, adjust the advisory size and parallelism settings against observed shuffle bytes.

title: A date filter eliminates entire input partitions
section: Adaptive plans, schemas, and file scans
steps:
The driver's optimizer separates eligible partition-key predicates from data predicates. For this catalog rule the filter must be suitable for pruning; Python UDFs and subqueries are not used by this rule.

For the date predicate Spark asks the catalog file index for matching partitions, replaces the relation's file index, and updates its estimated size.

Scan tasks need not open the excluded dates' files. The amount predicate may still benefit from Parquet filtering, but it does not identify directories by date.
trigger: A V1 catalog-backed Parquet table is partitioned by sale_date. Compare WHERE sale_date = DATE '2026-11-24' with a filter only on the non-partition amount column.
clue: Compare PartitionFilters in explain("formatted") and the scan's file metrics. PushedFilters is not proof of directory pruning.
repro: Create a disposable V1 catalog Parquet table partitioned by sale_date with two dates. Compare a date equality predicate with an amount-only predicate; inspect explain('formatted') and scan file counts after execution.
fix: Use a direct predicate on the partition key where it expresses the requested rows. Verify only the intended dates are read and keep any necessary data-column filter; predicate pushdown and directory pruning are different.

title: One Parquet file has an incompatible column type
section: Adaptive plans, schemas, and file scans
steps:
The driver supplies the read schema. An executor's vectorized Parquet reader chooses a column updater using both the file's physical type and Spark's requested type.

For an unsupported conversion the reader throws rather than silently casting. The scan reports a failure with the offending path and column. Retrying identical bytes cannot fix it.

The writer or batch must be identified: this is not a missing file, and skipping files can silently remove revenue from an otherwise successful report.
trigger: The report requests amount INT, but one batch of Parquet files contains a string amount. The file exists and its footer is readable.
clue: Compare the expected and actual types in the error with the schema of the offending file alone. count() can prune the column; materialize the values.
repro: Write a scratch Parquet file with a string amount of '42' and read it with spark.read.schema('amount INT').parquet(path).select('amount').collect(), with the vectorized reader enabled. Contrast with reading the file's native string schema.
fix: Read each compatible batch with its native schema, validate values, cast to the canonical type, and rewrite to a new path. Read that output back and check the type, count and total (42 for this fixture). Merely disabling vectorization is not a schema repair.

title: An input file disappears after listing
section: Adaptive plans, schemas, and file scans
steps:
The scan task opens the planned file lazily. A missing path raises FileNotFoundException, which the scan treats separately from a corrupt record or file.

With ignoreMissingFiles=true, it logs Skipped missing file and advances. With that option false, a missing file is not excused just because ignoreCorruptFiles=true.

Skipping makes a successful action possible without that file's rows. It does not restore the file or grant blanket permission to ignore access-control or missing HDFS-block errors.
trigger: A V1 file scan lists a partition successfully; another process removes a data file before its executor task opens it. The operator enables ignoreCorruptFiles and expects success.
clue: Compare executor warnings with the file listing and result counts. A green job after enabling the option is not evidence that the input snapshot was complete.
repro: Write two nonempty data files to a scratch directory. Supply an explicit schema, create the DataFrame and inspect inputFiles() to force listing; move one data file aside, then materialize a data column. Compare runs with ignoreMissingFiles off and on, restoring the fixture before each listing.
fix: Publish immutable input snapshots or coordinate retention with readers. Restore the missing file and verify the full expected row count; enable skipping only if partial results are explicitly acceptable.

title: A rerun succeeds without writing anything
steps:
The driver's file-write command checks whether the destination exists.

With ErrorIfExists, an existing path raises an error. With Ignore, the same test makes doInsertion false and Spark skips the file-write path.

No new output tasks need be launched for the skipped write. Spark did not read the existing dataset to confirm that it contains the expected date, rows, or schema.
trigger: A V1 Parquet batch is rerun against an existing output directory, once with the default error-if-exists mode and once with .mode("ignore").
clue: A successful return with unchanged files is expected under ignore. Unlike case 18, this can happen before any task or job commit. It is not a content-based deduplication or concurrency guarantee.
repro: Write a one-row Parquet dataset to a fresh path; attempt a different two-row write to that same path in default mode, then in ignore mode. Read back the path each time.
fix: If a rerun should replace data, use an explicit publication policy and validate its scope first. Confirm the intended values after reading back; ignore should preserve the original one-row content.

title: Overwrite replaces only the dates written
steps:
The driver recognizes overwrite with dynamic partition columns and dynamic overwrite mode. It doesn't delete matching directories up front; it uses staging for the new files.

Write tasks report which partition paths they actually produced. At job commit the driver's commit protocol collects those paths and replaces those partitions' directories.

Tuesday's old data remains. Conversely, old Monday rows not included in the new Monday output are not merged back: the unit being replaced is the partition, not an individual row.
trigger: An HDFS-backed V1 table is partitioned by date. A dynamic partition overwrite writes rows for Monday and Wednesday but none for Tuesday. The Hadoop file committer supports this mode.
clue: Inspect the dates present in the input and the destination before and after commit. This is neither full-root overwrite nor a transactional upsert; commit behavior depends on the filesystem and committer.
repro: Write Monday and Tuesday to a scratch partitionBy('day') Parquet dataset. Overwrite it with only Monday and Wednesday using .option('partitionOverwriteMode','dynamic') and a supporting committer.
fix: Use dynamic overwrite for replacement of touched dates, not per-row merge or full refresh. Verify Monday is replaced, Tuesday unchanged, Wednesday added; reconcile keys if duplicates or row-level updates matter.

title: One successful task creates three data files
steps:
The driver's file writer resolves the write option, falling back to the SQL configuration if the option is absent, and puts that limit in the description sent to tasks.

The executor writer counts records in the current file. Before writing the next row after reaching the cap, it closes that writer, increments the file counter, and opens another.

This one task writes 1,000 + 1,000 + 500 rows to three files. No extra Spark partition, executor, or speculative attempt is needed.
trigger: A single successful V1 writer task receives 2,500 rows for an unpartitioned output directory with .option("maxRecordsPerFile", 1000).
clue: Compare data filenames with distinct c000, c001, c002 counters against the single successful task in the Stages UI. The cap limits rows, not file size in bytes; exclude markers such as _SUCCESS when counting data files.
repro: Run spark.range(2500, numPartitions=1).write.option('maxRecordsPerFile',1000).parquet(path) on a fresh scratch path. Group the read-back rows by input_file_name() and count each group.
fix: If rollover alone created unwanted tiny files, raise or remove the cap and repeat in a new directory. Verify counts of 1,000/1,000/500 before and 2,500 total after; for many writer tasks also inspect partitioning.
